questions.s: General plan of the autonomic system (Last's):
o: Grey rami carry postganglionic efferent fibres

Grey rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibres from the trunk ganglia back into every spinal nerve.
They are present at all levels.
White rami carry preganglionic and visceral afferent fibres

White rami (T1 to L2 only) carry myelinated preganglionic fibres to the trunk and visceral afferents back to the cord.
So white rami are limited to the outflow segments.
The suprarenal glands receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply

The suprarenals and gonads have only sympathetic supply.
No parasympathetic fibres reach them.
Parasympathetic fibres supply the limbs

Parasympathetic supply is wholly visceral; no parasympathetic fibres supply the limbs.
All limb autonomic supply is sympathetic.

questions.s: Last's notes that lumbar sympathectomy at L1:
o: May compromise ejaculation

Sympathetic fibres from L1 contract the ductus deferens and seminal vesicles, so removing that ganglion can abolish ejaculation (emission).
Bilateral L1 sympathectomy is avoided in young men.
Abolishes bladder emptying

Bladder emptying depends on the parasympathetic detrusor supply, so lumbar sympathectomy does not abolish it.
The detrusor is S2 to S4.
Abolishes penile erection

Erection is parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic), so sympathectomy does not abolish it.
"Point and shoot": parasympathetic points, sympathetic shoots.
Removes vasoconstrictor supply to parts of the lower limb

Grey rami to the lumbar nerves carry vasoconstrictor fibres to the lower limb, so sympathectomy removes this supply and increases skin blood flow.
That is its purpose in vascular disease.
Each has parasympathetic, sympathetic and sensory roots

Each of the cranial parasympathetic ganglia (ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular and otic) receives a parasympathetic, a sympathetic and a sensory root.
Only the first synapses.
Only the parasympathetic fibres synapse in them

Sympathetic and sensory fibres pass straight through the cranial ganglia; only parasympathetic preganglionic fibres relay there.
A rule worth memorising.
The dorsal vagal nucleus relays in a named cranial ganglion

Fibres from the dorsal vagal nucleus relay in ganglia in the walls of the viscera, not in a named cranial ganglion.
The vagus has no named head ganglion for its efferents.
The sympathetic roots come from T5 to T8

The sympathetic roots of the cranial ganglia come from T1 to T3, relaying in the superior cervical ganglion.
T5 to T8 supply the abdomen.

questions.s: Sympathetic roots of the cranial ganglia (Last's):
o: The ciliary ganglion receives sympathetics from the ICA plexus

Postganglionic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the ciliary ganglion from the internal carotid plexus.
They then pass to dilator pupillae and vessels.
The otic ganglion receives sympathetics with the middle meningeal artery

The otic ganglion receives its sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the middle meningeal artery.
A branch of the external carotid system.
The submandibular ganglion receives sympathetics from the ICA plexus

The submandibular ganglion receives sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery (external carotid), not the internal carotid plexus.
External carotid ganglia: otic and submandibular.
The pterygopalatine ganglion receives sympathetics with the maxillary artery

The pterygopalatine ganglion receives sympathetic fibres via the deep petrosal nerve from the internal carotid plexus, not with the maxillary artery.
The deep petrosal joins the greater petrosal at foramen lacerum.
Its parasympathetic root is the lesser petrosal nerve

The parasympathetic root of the otic ganglion is the lesser petrosal nerve, carrying fibres from the inferior salivary nucleus via IX.
For the parotid.
It has a somatic motor root from the nerve to medial pterygoid

The otic ganglion has a somatic motor root from the nerve to medial pterygoid, unique among the cranial ganglia.
Its fibres pass to the two tensors.
Its secretomotor fibres reach the parotid via the facial nerve

Secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion reach the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve, not the facial nerve.
VII only passes through the gland.
Motor fibres to tensor tympani synapse in it

Motor fibres to tensor tympani pass through the otic ganglion without synapse.
Somatic motor fibres never synapse in autonomic ganglia.
The ciliary parasympathetic root comes via the nerve to inferior oblique

Edinger–Westphal fibres travel in the inferior division of III and leave in the nerve to inferior oblique to reach the ciliary ganglion.
This is its parasympathetic root.
The ciliary sensory root comes from the nasociliary nerve

The sensory root of the ciliary ganglion comes from the nasociliary nerve; its fibres pass through to the eyeball and cornea.
So the corneal reflex can use them.
The pterygopalatine sensory root comes from the mandibular nerve

The sensory root of the pterygopalatine ganglion comes from the maxillary nerve (its ganglionic branches), not the mandibular nerve.
The ganglion hangs from V2.
Pterygopalatine postganglionic lacrimal fibres travel in the nasociliary nerve

Postganglionic lacrimal fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion travel via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves, not the nasociliary nerve.
The nasociliary is sensory to the eye.
Cranial visceral afferent cell bodies lie in the inferior ganglia of IX and X

The visceral afferents of IX and X have cell bodies in their inferior ganglia and end centrally in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
Like dorsal root ganglia for the cranial nerves.
Pelvic visceral afferent cell bodies lie in the S2-4 posterior root ganglia

Pelvic visceral afferents have cell bodies in the S2 to S4 posterior root ganglia and serve bladder reflexes and pelvic pain.
They travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves.
Cranial visceral afferents end in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

Cranial visceral afferents end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius, not the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
The dorsal motor nucleus is purely efferent.
About 10% of abdominal vagal fibres are afferent

About 90 percent of abdominal vagal fibres are afferent, not 10 percent.
The vagus is mainly sensory.
It enters behind the medial arcuate ligament

The lumbar sympathetic trunk passes behind the medial arcuate ligament, on the front of psoas, to enter the abdomen.
It continues the thoracic trunk. (Last's p. 365)
The right trunk lies behind the IVC

The right lumbar trunk lies behind the IVC; the left lies alongside the aorta, with para-aortic nodes in front.
So the right is harder to find surgically. (Last's p. 365)
The common iliac vessels lie behind the trunks at the pelvic brim

The common iliac vessels lie in front of the trunks at the pelvic brim.
The trunks pass behind them into the pelvis. (Last's p. 365)
There are usually six lumbar ganglia

There are usually four lumbar ganglia, not six.
Fusion reduces their number. (Last's p. 365)

questions.s: Branches of the lumbar sympathetic trunk (Last's):
o: Grey rami pass to all five lumbar nerves

Every lumbar nerve receives a grey ramus, but only L1 and L2 send white rami.
Grey rami go everywhere; white rami only from the outflow segments. (Last's p. 365)
The superior hypogastric plexus lies in front of L5

Fibres from the aortic plexus and the L3 and L4 splanchnic nerves form the superior hypogastric plexus in front of L5. Last's notes it is misnamed the "presacral nerve".
It lies in front of the lumbosacral junction. (Last's p. 365)
White rami reach all five lumbar nerves

White rami reach only the first two lumbar nerves (L1 and L2), not all five.
The sympathetic outflow ends at L2. (Last's p. 365)
The "presacral nerve" lies in front of the sacrum

Last's says "presacral nerve" is a misnomer: the plexus is prelumbar, in front of L5, not the sacrum.
It divides below into the hypogastric nerves. (Last's p. 365)
The lesser splanchnic nerve comes from T10 and T11

The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from the T10 and T11 ganglia; the greater from T5 to T9; and the least from T12.
Each pierces the crus. (Last's p. 365)
The least splanchnic relays in a renal ganglion

The least splanchnic nerve relays in a small renal ganglion behind the renal artery, an offshoot of the coeliac ganglion.
It supplies the kidney. (Last's p. 365)
The greater splanchnic nerve comes from T1 to T4

The greater splanchnic nerve comes from T5 to T9, not T1 to T4.
T1 to T4 supply the head, neck, upper limb and heart. (Last's p. 365)
Coeliac fibres to the suprarenal medulla are the secretomotor supply

Preganglionic splanchnic fibres reach the suprarenal medulla without relaying and are its secretomotor supply. Postganglionic coeliac fibres to the gland are vasomotor.
The medulla is a modified ganglion. (Last's p. 365)
The parasympathetic is the main motor supply to the bladder

The pelvic splanchnic (parasympathetic) fibres are the main motor supply of the bladder; sympathetic fibres are vasomotor and inhibit the detrusor.
Hence parasympathetic damage causes retention. (Last's p. 380)
Sympathetic fibres contract the superficial trigone

Sympathetic fibres contract the superficial trigone and, in the male, the internal sphincter.
This closes the bladder neck during ejaculation. (Last's p. 380)
Bladder distension sensation travels with sympathetic fibres

Bladder distension sensation travels with the parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) fibres, not the sympathetic.
The sympathetic carries some pain from the bladder roof. (Last's p. 380)
Rectal pain travels only with sympathetic fibres

Rectal pain travels with both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres, not only sympathetic.
The rectum is a transitional zone. (Last's p. 380)
